summary: Defines the Local Mail Transfer Protocol, a variation on SMTP for handing mail to a final delivery system without a mail queue. SMTP servers must manage queues, which is unnecessary for plain local delivery.

eli5.summary: SMTP is like a mail truck that must keep undelivered letters. LMTP is for the last step, where the mailbox either takes the letter or says no.

subtitle: A variant of SMTP for handing mail to a delivery system that keeps no queue, with one reply per recipient.

tldr.problem: SMTP returns only one reply for a whole message, so a server given several recipients must queue the message and retry the ones that fail temporarily. Simple local delivery agents should not have to run a queue.
tldr.mechanism: LMTP is SMTP with a few changes: the LHLO command replaces HELO and EHLO, and after the final dot of DATA the server sends one reply for each recipient that was accepted.
tldr.outcome: The client keeps the queue and retries, and the delivery agent only reports per-recipient results. LMTP is for specific prior arrangement and must not be used on TCP port 25.

today: RFC 2033 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why SMTP Forces a Queue
sections.content:
In SMTP a single mail transaction can name several recipients, but the final . of the DATA command gets only one reply code for the whole transaction. If delivery to the first recipient works and delivery to the second hits a temporary failure, there is no way to tell the client. The server has to queue the message and try the second recipient again later.

That is useful for store-and-forward relaying between hosts, which is what SMTP was designed for. In some limited situations, outside mail exchange between independent hosts on public networks, it is better for the server not to manage a queue and for the client to do that work instead.
sections.eli5: If you hand a helper two letters and they can only answer yes or no for both, they must keep the one they could not deliver. LMTP lets them answer separately for each letter.

sections.title: Where LMTP Fits in a Mail System
sections.content:
The RFC describes a hypothetical host with three subsystems. A queue manager speaks ordinary SMTP on TCP port 25 and keeps the mail queue in persistent storage. Two delivery agents handle addresses in the host's own domains: one is a gateway to another mail system, the other delivers into a persistent mail spool.

Using SMTP over a local inter-process channel to reach the delivery agents would make each agent manage its own queue. The common alternative, starting an agent with the addresses as command-line arguments and reading one exit code, has three problems: one exit code applies to all recipients, it is hard to extend for ESMTP features such as DSN and ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, and exits caused by system libraries on temporary conditions are often read as permanent errors.

LMTP is used on the connections from the queue manager to the delivery agents. It is not useful toward the queue manager, because the queue manager has a queue and can take responsibility for later delivery.
sections.eli5: A big post office sorts and holds mail. The little desks that put letters into boxes do not want to hold anything, so they just say 'done' or 'not now' for each letter.

sections.title: LHLO and the Changed Commands
sections.content:
LMTP is identical to SMTP and its service extensions except as this document changes it. The HELO and EHLO commands are replaced by LHLO, which has the same semantics as EHLO. Using a different command lets a misconfiguration be detected when the two sides are not speaking the same protocol.

An LMTP server MUST NOT return a Positive Completion reply to HELO or EHLO; the 500 reply code is recommended. A Positive Completion reply is one whose first digit is 2, and a successful RCPT is one that returns such a reply.
sections.eli5: LMTP uses a different secret hello word, so if someone says the wrong hello, both sides notice they are talking to the wrong kind of friend.

sections.title: One Reply per Recipient
sections.content:
If no RCPT command succeeded in the transaction, DATA MUST fail with a 503 reply. Otherwise, after the final . the server returns one reply for each earlier successful RCPT, in the order the commands were issued, even when the same forward-path was given more than once. A multiline reply counts as a single reply.

A Positive Completion reply means the server accepts responsibility for delivering or relaying the message to that recipient, and it MUST NOT lose the message for frivolous reasons such as a later host crash or a predictable resource shortage.

If the server supports the CHUNKING extension, a BDAT command with the LAST parameter behaves the same way, returning zero replies if there were no successful RCPT commands. BDAT without LAST still returns exactly one reply.
sections.eli5: After the letter is handed over, the helper answers once for each person on the list, in the same order, saying 'delivered' or 'try again later'.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
LMTP MUST NOT be used on TCP service port 25. A server MUST implement the PIPELINING and ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES extensions and SHOULD implement 8BITMIME. LMTP SHOULD NOT be used over wide area networks, and a server that can quickly accept responsibility for multiple recipients and send any needed notifications SHOULD NOT implement LMTP at all. These rules limit the duplicate-message problem described in RFC 1047.

The server SHOULD send each reply as soon as possible, flushing its output buffer if the next recipient will take a while. The client SHOULD process replies as they arrive. If the connection closes after only some replies have arrived, the client MUST process those and treat the remaining recipients as temporary failures.

The RFC says it has no known security issues.
sections.eli5: The rules say: answer quickly, keep this for short local trips, and if the line goes dead, treat the unanswered letters as 'try again later'.
